opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. That's a fun question, because I didn't really notice the difference until I'd lived with both.

The East Coast, at least the parts I experienced, felt more rooted in tradition. There's a strong sense that ideas have a lineage: you read the foundational papers, you understand why things were built the way they were, and you earn the right to have an opinion. That gave me a lot of respect for rigor and for thinking carefully before speaking. Theory matters there, and so does history.

When I moved to the West Coast, especially into the Bay Area AI world, the energy was completely different. People ask "what if we just built it?" before they ask "has anyone proven this is possible?" It's very optimistic and fast. You see someone release an open-source project on a weekend, and by Monday thousands of people are using it. That changed how I thought about impact. It wasn't just about writing a good paper; it was about whether the thing I made could actually reach people and be useful.

Having both cultures shaped how I relate to the wider world. The East Coast side made me cautious about hype and want to understand things deeply. The West Coast side pushed me to engage, to ship things, to put work out in public and let the community react. In systems work like serving large language models, you need both. You need rigor so the system is correct and efficient, and you need that builder mentality so it gets adopted and improved by an open community.

I also think the West Coast made me more comfortable being connected to people globally. Open source is borderless. Contributors come from China, Europe, everywhere. That made me feel less like I belonged to one academic tradition and more like part of a big, messy, collaborative effort. Honestly, that's been one of the most rewarding parts of my journey.

r001.rationale: The response describes East Coast rigor and West Coast building and impact, but does not communicate a growing pressure around personal success.

r002.rationale: It says the West Coast encouraged engagement and global connection, but does not say Ying wanted to be detached from the wider world on the East Coast.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. That's an interesting question, because I think most people assume the East Coast and the West Coast split is about finance versus tech, or old money versus new money. For me it was really about how people relate to ideas.

When I was on the East Coast, in a more academic, theory-driven environment, the question was always "is this true, and can you prove it?" There was a lot of respect for depth, for rigor, for spending years on one problem. That shaped me a lot. It made me careful. It made me suspicious of hype, which turned out to be a useful instinct later.

Then I came to the Bay Area, and the question flipped. It became "does this work, and who is using it?" Nobody cared if your idea was elegant if you couldn't ship it. At first that was uncomfortable. I remember feeling like people were being sloppy. But over time I realized it was a different kind of rigor. The feedback loop is the world itself. You put something out, people either adopt it or they don't, and that teaches you things no proof ever could.

So in terms of my relationship to the wider world, I'd say the East Coast taught me to think for myself and not to trust something just because it's popular. The West Coast taught me that ideas are social. Open source especially drove that home. You write some code, and then suddenly there are people in Shanghai, Berlin, Bangalore filing issues and sending patches at three in the morning. Your work stops being yours. It becomes a conversation.

I think the healthiest version of me is somewhere in between. Deep enough to know when something is actually right, and open enough to put it out before it's perfect and let the world tell me what I missed.

r001.rationale: The response discusses rigor, hype, and shipping ideas, but does not identify growing pressure around personal success.

r002.rationale: It describes West Coast ideas as social and globally shared, but does not say Ying Sheng wanted detachment from the wider world on the East Coast.

astra-6.text:
I think the difference is partly in how people relate to established ideas. The East Coast intellectual culture, as I see it, puts more emphasis on history, institutions, and understanding how an argument fits into a longer conversation. The West Coast feels more willing to ask, “What if we tried something different? Could we build it?” Those are broad impressions, of course, and there are plenty of exceptions.

For me, those perspectives offer a useful tension. One encourages you to recognize that the world has a history, and that your own experience is only a small part of it. The other encourages you to feel that you can participate—that you don’t have to accept everything as it is. I think a healthy relationship to the wider world needs both: curiosity about why things are the way they are, and a willingness to help change them.

r001.rationale: The response discusses broad differences between East Coast and West Coast intellectual cultures but does not identify growing pressure around personal success in Ying Sheng’s experience.

r002.rationale: It describes West Coast culture as encouraging participation and change, but does not say Ying Sheng wanted to be detached from the wider world on the East Coast or renewed that desire to engage on the West Coast.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the difference is partly about how you relate to ideas. On the East Coast, I felt more of an emphasis on understanding where an idea comes from—its history, its intellectual context, the arguments around it. On the West Coast, the question felt more like, “What can you do with this? What could you build?”

Those environments encouraged different ways of engaging with the wider world. One made me more attentive to context and complexity; the other encouraged me to participate, to try things before I felt I understood everything. I value that tension. You want enough historical awareness to question your assumptions, but also enough confidence to act while your understanding is still incomplete.

r001.rationale: The response describes West Coast encouragement to build and act, but does not identify pressure around personal success.

r002.rationale: It says the West Coast encouraged participation, but does not describe Ying Sheng wanting to be detached from the wider world on the East Coast.
